📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AC Milan and Juventus are both keeping tabs on Benjamin Sesko’s situation at Manchester United, according to a report.

United paid around €80m to sign Sesko from RB Leipzig, hoping he would be the long-term fix for the No.9 position. Last season he performed reasonably well, scoring 11 goals in 30 Premier League games which was not bad for a 22-year-old in a newly introduced league.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

This season, however, he is stuck on one goal in four league games, having spent time out injured too. With significant changes at Old Trafford – including the arrival of Mauricio Pochettino as the head coach – it is another blank slate for the squad.

For example, club captain Bruno Fernandes has been linked with a move to Milan. Now, according to journalist Alessandro Jacobone, a new idea has emerged for the centre-forward position, perhaps if the pursuit of Nicolo Tresoldi does not go to proposal.

“Juve and Milan are keeping an eye on things. But summer is the most realistic scenario. Benjamin Šeško could leave Manchester United, with Juventus and Milan having already made some preliminary enquiries to assess the financial feasibility of a potential move,” he stated.

“For now, these are only preliminary discussions, useful for finding out the figures, conditions and possible deal structures. No concrete negotiations have been initiated.

“Sources close to the player’s camp are also playing down the possibility of a transfer as early as January, making a potential move in the next summer window considerably more likely. One to watch.”.

Four of those 11 goals in his debut campaign came off the bench too as he developed a knack for being an impact substitute. This could give Milan food for thought, given they are looking for an alter-ego to Goncalo Ramos rather than someone to solely take over the striker role.

Nations League quarter-final draw: Why England are favourites to win the tournament

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 09:00, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:00.
  • England should be seen as the favourites to win the UEFA Nations League ahead of the quarter-final draw, a former Three Lions striker has exclusively told Sports Mole.
  • Thomas Tuchel's side will learn their knockout fate on Friday morning when the draw for the last eight is held, and England head into the ceremony as one of the four seeded teams courtesy of finishing first in League A Group 3.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 09:00, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:00.

England should be seen as the favourites to win the UEFA Nations League ahead of the quarter-final draw, a former Three Lions striker has exclusively told Sports Mole.

Thomas Tuchel's side will learn their knockout fate on Friday morning when the draw for the last eight is held, and England head into the ceremony as one of the four seeded teams courtesy of finishing first in League A Group 3.

The Three Lions unexpectedly pipped world and European champions Spain to top spot courtesy of an engrossing 3-2 win over La Roja on Sunday, ending an unparalleled 43-game unbeaten run for Luis de la Fuente's side.

England will meet one of Belgium, Netherlands or Norway in the quarter-finals, while France, Portugal and Germany represent the other three Group A winners going for glory.

Despite the strength of the draw, former England striker Mark Hateley believes that Tuchel's men have made themselves the favourites to win the trophy for the first time, and also reserved special praise foe the goalkeeping heroics of James Trafford.

Asked if England are leading the charge for Nations League stardom, Hateley replied: "100%. That's the best I've seen England, or any team, play over a period of, say, 60 minutes.

"They were incredible: high press, press, press, press, going man for man, confident enough to go man for man at the back against the world champions, allowing your midfield players to jump up with the strikers.

According to recent reports, “It was tremendous to watch, the very best we've seen from an England side for many, many years, honestly. It was superb. We went to 3-0, rightly so, and Spain never had a shot. Their first was 50 minutes in, in the second half.

“Trafford must have thought 'this was a goddamn easy game.' The only time I think he was at fault was his starting position for the penalty, when Anderson brought the boy down. If his starting position had been higher, I think he'd have made the interception. That would be my only fault for the goalkeeper.

“If you’re a shot stopper, you’re a shot stopper - it’s just the other side of his game, where you're reading it and where you should be, playing as that sweeper.

Industry observers note that "With the way we were pressing, the only ball really on for Spain was a ball in behind into the last third, which was empty for long periods. There was nobody there where I thought he could have been. But those are the things you pick up on and learn from.”.

England have only ever competed in the Nations League knockout stages once before in the inaugural 2018-19 edition, when they reached the finals courtesy of beating Spain and Croatia to first place in their group.

However, at a time when the Nations League Finals only comprised four teams, Gareth Southgate's side fell to a 3-1 loss to the Netherlands in the semi-finals, meaning that they are still awaiting their first knockout-phase win in the tournament.

England could only place third in the group stage of the 2020-21 tournament, before an embarrassing relegation to League B in the 2022-23 edition, although they swiftly returned to the top tier.

In the current format, England's record of five wins, one loss and 19 goals scored represented their best-ever performance in the group stage of the Nations League, fuelling the belief that the Three Lions can finally end their trophy drought in 2027.

Mark Hateley was speaking to Sports Mole on behalf of London.bet.

Bologna vs Udinese - prediction, team news, lineups

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Jonathan O'Shea | 20 Nov 2026 09:03, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:08.
  • Aiming to pick up where they left off before the break, Bologna will host Serie A's bottom side when Udinese visit Stadio Dall'Ara on Sunday.
  • After a sticky start, both clubs have already changed coaches, and the Rossoblu's latest boss has sparked a surge up the standings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 20 Nov 2026 09:03, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:08.

Aiming to pick up where they left off before the break, Bologna will host Serie A's bottom side when Udinese visit Stadio Dall'Ara on Sunday.

After a sticky start, both clubs have already changed coaches, and the Rossoblu's latest boss has sparked a surge up the standings.

Since Raffaele Palladino's arrival midway through September, Bologna have been a team transformed, winning five games from six and climbing towards the European places.

The Emilian club signed off for the international break with a run of four consecutive wins, with the highlight being a 4-2 victory over AC Milan at San Siro.

Last time out, the Rossoblu's revival continued in the Derby dell'Emilia against Parma, as their hosts were swiftly reduced to 10 men and ultimately suffered a 2-1 defeat.

So, having won none of their first five games during the short-lived Domenico Tedesco era, Bologna are now one of Serie A's form sides.

However, Palladino must still work on their awful home record, which stretches back through most of last season; so far this term, they have claimed five points from a possible 15 at the Dall'Ara.

Either home or away, Udinese have picked up just one from their last nine matches and are therefore stuck at the foot of the table.

The Bianconeri have put a meagre five points on the board so far, slumping into an unexpected crisis.

Safe mid-table finishers in back-to-back seasons under Kosta Runjaic, this campaign has completely unravelled, and even a change of coach has yet to produce results.

Just before the break, new boss Paolo Zanetti lost his first game against former club Venezia, with Udinese going down 2-1 in a crucial battle at the bottom.

Now, desperately needing some success, Zanetti must meet Palladino for the seventh time in management - to date, the pair have three wins apiece.

Unfortunately for fans of the Friulani, recent history is not on their side: they have won none of the last five meetings with Bologna, failing to even score in each of the last three.

Though Bologna will be without injured trio Jay Enem, Juan Miranda and Emil Holm, left-winger Nicolo Cambiaghi has resumed training after leaving Italy's UEFA Nations League camp.

Having impressed in the Azzurri's win over France, Cambiaghi has overcome a minor ankle problem and should start alongside Federico Bernadeschi in the final third.

The latter has previously scored four goals against Udinese, finding the net as a substitute in both of the last two meetings.

Bernardeschi and Samuel Mbangula - who recently hit a hat-trick at San Siro - are the hosts' joint-top Serie A scorers with three goals each; Jurgen Ekkelenkamp has netted three times for Udinese.

The visitors must travel without Nicolo Bertola, who has suffered a thigh injury in training and joins Idrissa Gueye on the sidelines.

In better news for Zanetti, David Alaba could return from his latest layoff, while Nicolo Zaniolo is available after withdrawing from the Italy squad for personal reasons.

Set to support Keinan Davis up front, Zaniolo has played eight league games against Bologna without ever scoring.

Bologna possible starting lineup:.

Skorupski; Darmian, Casale, Theate; Zortea, Ferguson, Pobega, Alhassane; Bernardeschi, Cambiaghi; Odgaard.

Udinese possible starting lineup:.

Okoye; Abankwah, Palma, Solet; Vojvoda, Karlstrom, Piotrowski, Kamara; Zaniolo, Ekkelenkamp; Davis.

Bologna may be in fine form but they tend to falter on home turf, while Udinese are struggling to pick up points anywhere.

Only Sassuolo have conceded more goals than the Friulani, and the Rossoblu have kept just a single clean sheet, so a score-draw could be on the cards.

#26546. Latest Update: Man United's first woman on their backroom team, the fitness enforcer, a scorpion-kicking goalkeeper coach... and his son! Meet Mauricio Pochettino's team of experts flying in to whip United's flops into shape

Latest Update: Man United's first woman on their backroom team, the fitness enforcer, a scorpion-kicking goalkeeper coach... and his son! Meet Mauricio Pochettino's team of experts flying in to whip United's flops into shape

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 21:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 07:43 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Mauricio Pochettino will have little time to waste when he takes to Manchester United's training ground for the first time on Wednesday, just days ahead of their trip to bitter rivals Liverpool.
  • The Argentine, however, will not be doing it alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By KIERAN GILL, MAIL SPORT REPORTER.

Published: 21:00 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 07:43 EST, 17 November 2026.

Mauricio Pochettino will have little time to waste when he takes to Manchester United's training ground for the first time on Wednesday, just days ahead of their trip to bitter rivals Liverpool.

The Argentine, however, will not be doing it alone. With him, Pochettino brings to Old Trafford an experienced and familiar cast of trusted colleagues, who will be tasked with supporting him in his mission to turn things around in Manchester.

From a first-team coach who has known him since 1992 to the boss' own son, Daily Mail Sport takes a look at the backroom staff accompanying Pochettino at United...

Sources indicate that when the Manchester United reporters turn up for press conferences at Carrington, they will notice one seat, usually in the front row and to the far left, has a reserved sign on it. It will be for Perez, who is Pochettino’s eyes and ears. Those same correspondents may well be followed by Perez on social media, so he can stay in the loop of what is being written.

According to recent reports, wherever Pochettino goes, so too does his shadow Perez. You have probably already heard about the time Pochettino met his idol Sir Alex Ferguson for lunch in London back in 2016. What you may not know is that Perez was there, too. He and Pochettino have been joined at the hip ever since they met in Barcelona when one was an analyst and the other was managing Espanyol.

Mauricio Pochettino (right) arrives at Manchester United with a trusted team of backroom staff.

According to recent reports, that was in 2010. Perez had studied sports science at university and completed his coaching qualifications but was considering quitting football. Pochettino convinced him otherwise, and they soon learned they shared the same principles, including the importance of creating the right culture of togetherness within a club to succeed.

According to recent reports, in 2013, it was Perez’s turn to convince Pochettino. The Argentinian was unsure about moving to England to manage Southampton, but the Spaniard had spent a month on these shores studying how Premier League sides train and play.

He told Pochettino that the intensity of his sessions and style would fit perfectly and that he could not turn down the chance to take on the Premier League.

Recent findings suggest that they now consider each other family, and Perez’s story itself is a nice one. By his own admission, he will tell you he failed at becoming a professional player, but he believes the way in which he worked his way in as a coach can inspire others who dream of finding their own place in football.

He loves the game, so much so that he would use days off to travel from London to Manchester to visit the National Football Museum. Now he will be living much closer to his favourite hotspot.

As well as being the glue which connects various club departments together, Perez is a fitness and conditioning specialist, and a normal working day might involve him arriving at the training ground at 7.30am.

Industry observers note that after meeting with Pochettino over breakfast, he will then hold a 9am medical meeting where plans for each player are discussed and decided. Programmes tend to be tailored to individuals rather than set for the whole squad. Perez was credited with helping to establish Southampton and Tottenham Hotspur as among the fittest teams in the Premier League.

Where Pochettino is larger than life, Perez is unassuming, and has never sought to step into management as he prefers to work in the shadows.

Jesus Perez, pictured with Pochettino at Spurs in 2019, has long been his right-hand man.

We talk about Pochettino’s man-management prowess, but the same is true of Perez.

For example, when Chelsea beat Leicester City 4-2 in an FA Cup quarter-final in 2023-24, Raheem Sterling had a stinker. He missed a penalty, spurned a one-on-one and skied a free-kick. Chelsea’s fans booed him, and chanted ‘you don’t know what you’re doing’ at Pochettino when he substituted Mykhailo Mudryk rather than Sterling after 78 minutes at 2-2. Perez was the first to go straight to Sterling to put an arm around him that day.

And when Cole Palmer was becoming a household name in Pochettino’s one and only season at Chelsea, Perez was among those who privately tried to help the Englishman understand the perils of the distractions of his new-found fame.

According to recent reports, when they departed Chelsea, Pochettino and Perez were men of their word and honoured their commitment to manage the World XI in the Soccer Aid charity match a few weeks later. That was despite the awkwardness of the game being held at Stamford Bridge. They lost 6-3 to Frank Lampard’s England XI.

MIGUEL D’AGOSTINO, FIRST-TEAM COACH.

To give a sense of how long Pochettino has known ‘Miki’, around 1992, Pochettino purchased his first car while a player for Newell’s Old Boys. He gave his team-mate a lift home. When D’Agostino went to get out of the car, the wind caught it hard, and broke Pochettino’s door. D'Agostino never paid the bill to have it fixed – something Pochettino occasionally likes to remind him of.

Miguel D'Agostino, known as 'Miki', has heaps of experience as a former analyst and scout.

The first-team coach has known Pochettino since 1992 (both pictured at Tottenham in 2019).

Pochettino clearly forgave his fellow defender, who was also plying his trade under Marcelo Bielsa.

D’Agostino was an analyst at Espanyol, initially attached to the scouting department before assuming responsibility for filming training sessions and overseeing player analysis. From there, he followed Pochettino wherever he went, from Southampton to Tottenham to Paris Saint-Germain to Chelsea to the United States national team.

Sources indicate that while with the USA, D’Agostino would watch games in the MLS, going to Real Salt Lake or wherever there were players for scouting. In training, he is hands-on, sometimes with a stopwatch in hand or notepad containing that day’s drills.

When Pochettino tested positive for Covid-19 in January 2021, D’Agostino and Perez took temporary charge of his PSG side. They beat Angers 1-0 away from home in Ligue 1.

All of Pochettino’s confidants have a good grasp of English.

SILVIA TUYA, STRENGTH AND CONDITIONING COACH.

The newest member of Pochettino’s inner circle, having joined his USA national set-up in October 2024.

With a PhD in sports science, Tuya had worked with FC Levante Badalona in Liga F, Spain’s top tier for women’s football, while she also served as a lecturer at the National Institute of Physical Education of Catalonia at the University of Barcelona.

Since teaming up with Pochettino, she was seen on the training pitch and in the gym with the players.

Tuya will become Manchester United's first-ever female coach connected with the men's team.

Silvia Tuya is the newest member of Pochettino’s team, having joined his USA set-up in 2024.

Tuya is set to become Manchester United's first-ever female coach with the men's team.

TONI JIMENEZ, GOALKEEPING COACH.

After winning gold for Spain at the Barcelona Olympics in 1992, Jimenez met Pochettino in 1994 when they became team-mates for Espanyol, but it is worth recalling the 2000 Copa del Rey final when they found themselves on opposing sides.

The goalkeeper represented Atletico Madrid, and Pochettino was in defence for Espanyol, who won 2-1. After full-time, Pochettino delayed his celebrations to go and console his friend, who had already endured a challenging year with his father having passed away.

According to recent reports, jimenez has never forgotten that kindness from Pochettino, and like the others, the two have worked together wherever the latter has managed, from Espanyol to Southampton to Tottenham to PSG to Chelsea to the USA. They have shared a fair few of their favourite mate teas in their time, and now for United, where Jimenez will work with Senne Lammens and Co.

It has been revealed that they say training is rarely boring when Jimenez is involved. He was happy to prove to Tottenham’s players during one tour of Malaysia that he could copy Rene Higuita’s scorpion kick save, for example, and is pretty good when testing his goalkeepers in free-kick practice. Lammens should beware he is liable to do a little dance if he scores past you, however.

Hugo Lloris, the former Spurs goalkeeper who won the 2018 World Cup with France, frequently credited the charismatic Jimenez for adding new areas to his game. Pochettino has also hailed Jimenez for how he keeps second and third-choice goalkeepers motivated when they are not playing.

Hugo Lloris frequently credited Toni Jimenez (pictured) for adding new areas to his game.

Sebastiano Pochettino first worked with his father at Tottenham (pictured celebrating at PSG).

SEBASTIANO POCHETTINO, SPORTS SCIENTIST AND FITNESS COACH.

It has been revealed that the son of the manager. A graduate of Southampton Solent University, Sebastiano first worked with his father at Tottenham. It was said that he had become the Premier League’s youngest sports scientist when he was hired at the age of 22.

He soon became a regular sight in training sessions and on match days, seen putting the players through their paces and with the substitutes as they warmed up.

Industry observers note that sebastiano became a fitness coach and joined his old man at PSG, Chelsea and the USA. One of his specialties is in injury prevention, and that includes monitoring the players’ sleep and mood.

Trust is important to Pochettino, and he knows he can rely on family.

Hired by the USA as their men's national team lead analyst in August 2023 - just over a year before Pochettino took charge - Scott previously spent eight years at the FA before moving to Inter Miami.

He graduated from Liverpool John Moores University, achieving a first class BsC in Science and Football, with his major project titled 'A Comparison of the Technical Demands in Academy and Reserve Team Soccer'.

He went on to complete a PhD in Exercise Psychology & Performance Analysis there, before putting his skills to use during internships at Everton and Liverpool before joining the FA.

Scott has clearly impressed Pochettino, who confirmed before Tuesday's clash with Haiti that he was among those staying with him for that game before joining United - with Perez, Jimenez and Pochettino Jnr having travelled to England already.

Industry observers note that 'I am with Miguel and Silvia and Alec [for this game],' he remarked. 'After, they are going to join me in Manchester.'.

By Matt Law | 20 Nov 2026 09:23, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:23.

Barcelona will resume their 2026-27 La Liga campaign with a home fixture against Villarreal on Sunday afternoon.

Hansi Flick's side are currently top of the La Liga table, boasting a record of 11 wins and one defeat from their 12 matches to collect 33 points, which has left them three points ahead of second-placed Real Madrid at this stage of proceedings.

Barcelona have won their last three games in all competitions, including a 2-1 success over Atletico Madrid in their last fixture before the November international break.

Villarreal, meanwhile, have a record of four wins, three draws and five defeats from their 12 league matches this season to collect 15 points.

The Yellow Submarine are at the moment eighth in the division, three points behind sixth-placed Sevilla.

Here, Sports Mole looks at the head-to-head record between Barcelona and Villarreal ahead of their clash at Camp Nou this weekend.

Barcelona have tackled Villarreal on 58 occasions throughout history, and they comfortably lead the head-to-head record, posting 36 wins to Villarreal's 12, while there have also been 10 draws.

Lionel Messi is the all-time leading goalscorer in this fixture, having found the back of the net on 16 occasions against Villarreal during his time at Barcelona, while Neymar is second on nine.

As for the Yellow Submarine, former Manchester United and Atletico Madrid star Diego Forlan is their leading goalscorer against Barcelona, having netted five times against the Catalan outfit during his Villarreal career.

In La Liga, there have been 52 meetings, with Barcelona's winning 32 times to Villarreal's 11, while the points have been shared on nine occasions in Spain's top flight.

Villarreal incredibly recorded a 5-3 victory away to Barcelona in January 2024 and 3-2 win in May 2025, either side of a 5-1 triumph for the Catalan team in September 2024.

However, they were most recently downed 2-0 by La Blaugrana at Estadio de la Ceramica in December 2025, with centre-back Renato Veiga being sent off for a reckless tackle on Lamine Yamal, who went on to score the second for Hansi Flick's side.

Villarreal's last three wins over Barcelona have all come away from home, and they have not actually managed to beat the Catalan side in front of their own supporters since October 2007.

Barcelona's dominance in this fixture is perhaps best highlighted by the fact that they have won 12 of the last 15 La Liga meetings between the two clubs, even if Villarreal have enjoyed strong spells such as when they recorded three straight victories between April 2007 and March 2008.

The last meeting between the two sides took place at Camp Nou in February 2026, with Barcelona recording a 4-1 win.

Barcelona will now be looking to post a third straight victory over Villarreal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 125th cap was no different to the first for Harry Kane, who has now been in the business of goal accumulation for so long that it is only at the landmark moments, that all of us are obliged to step back and take in the full scale of the work he has created.

Peter Shilton took 20 years to rack up his 125 caps, while for Kane it has been just 11 – and then there are the goals. Two more on Tuesday took him to 91 which means that only 12 other England players in history have more England caps than Kane has England goals. This unassuming man from Chingford, who looks like a mildly rebellious academic from the late 1950s, was at it again: the first-time strike, the back-post header. He has some misses across these 11 years, most infamously from the penalty spot against France at the Qatar World Cup almost four years ago, so, yes, there are some regrets too. But what sticks is the way he has taken his chances – again and again.

Following his debut goal in 2015 against Lithuania, Kane has missed just 27 of the 152 England games since. He has added to the total like a great Test batsman patiently moving the scoreboard along. There was a bad run without goals in 2020 and before that in 2018. He scored only five in his first 17 caps and then scored 14 in his next 10. Against a very mediocre Czech Republic team this was classic late-era Kane, picking his moments and taking those chances with the usual absence of nerves. He was even substituted before the end.

It has been revealed that afterwards at a Wembley press conference to mark the occasion, he invoked the cricket analogy himself on the question of scoring 100 England goals. “Being in the 90s, I try not to think about it too much, and it’s like I guess being a cricketer in the 90s. The more you think about the hundred… you don’t always get there.” There has still not been the elusive major trophy in the Kane England years but there has been success relative to the three decades that came before it. Semi-finals, finals – a good team if not a winning team.

Sources indicate that at the centre of it has been a man around whom there has never been any scandal or, by the usual measure, much that might be described as spectacular. Rather it has been the scope of Kane’s career that is the most striking. The volume of the goals, of appearances, the capacity to be available – to play, to score – and the absolute quality of the player himself. He is determined to wring the very last drop out of his talent and usually refuses to acknowledge the prospect of the end, although there was a nod to it this time. “At some stage you know this opportunity isn’t going to be here,” he remarked. “I’m not going to be around forever, and I still hope that’s a long way away. But ultimately, of course, there’s times you’re tired or you’re injured, but I know I’ll miss it when it’s done. I try to always remind myself that and always try to make myself available.”.

It has been revealed that one expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he mentioned, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

It has been revealed that no team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

According to recent reports, england kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

The second goal, on 40 minutes, was one for the ages. Anderson’s ball out to the right was met first time by Rogers for the cross and Kane ran into the space, as he has done so many times, to deliver a finish struck with customary assuredness. Bellingham almost flicked in Rogers’s cross on 56 minutes and from the corner that came after, Kane nodded in a header at the back post from Lewis Hall’s cross. All said, the defending was woeful but there was nothing wrong with the finish.

Thomas Tuchel believes England have taken a step forward from their World Cup heartbreak over this international break and stated he was “honoured” to hear fans sing his name.

England finished their four Nations League games with a 3-0 win over Czech Republic, in which Harry Kane scored twice on his record-equalling 125th appearance.

It meant that Tuchel’s team have won three and lost one, against Spain, of their four games since the World Cup, after which the England head coach was heavily criticised for the semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Tuchel seems to have won the forgiveness of some England supporters, who sang his name at the start and the end of Tuesday’s game.

Recent findings suggest that “It means a lot,” Tuchel said. “It’s amazing to have a song. It’s the biggest honour. And I’m very happy and very honoured. They can be sure that I will give my absolute best to make our team win and play well.”.

In a recent development, asked if he sensed a change in mood around his England team since the fall-out from the World Cup, Tuchel stated: “I do and I think it’s necessary to move on. I think I can only repeat that we didn’t go out in the group stage. Sometimes it feels like that and we didn’t. As I said, our aim was always to progress, move forward and improve.”.

Tuchel snapped back at a reporter who questioned why he felt it necessary to repeat that England had not gone out in the group stage of the World Cup, claiming the criticism had felt a “little bit” too harsh.

But on whether England have shown they are a step ahead of where the team were at the World Cup during this international camp, Tuchel was far more positive and replied: “Of course and that’s what we have to do. That is our goal to constantly improve and develop.

Sources indicate that “We had these experiences together and we had a big tournament together, and it was very positive. It’s necessary to move forward and improve, especially in sports. This is what we’re trying to do.

Sources indicate that “We adjusted some details in our structure and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity, and on the togetherness of the team. The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch, and I think that’s what you could see.”.

Sources indicate that we played a very good match, very fluid and to put it into context it was the fourth match in 11 or 12 days. We dominated the whole match, had some good opportunities, scored some beautiful goals. Subs were strong. Very good performance again.

In a recent development, [Leading the way, Mr Kane] Of course. That’s what he does. I don’t take it for granted. It’s just exceptional, every single match. It’s just difficult to find fresh words to express it.

Training, attitude, cohesion, belief, of course [is why they’re stronger than ever].

According to recent reports, [Has the World Cup made England stronger?]  Of course, we got the first medal in 60 years. We didn’t go out in the group stage. We had a strong qualification, strong World Cup and strong camp. All four matches were on a high level. The camp throughout from the first day was on the highest level. You learn every day together. We grew stronger.

According to recent reports, I was happy that everyone who was in the camp was contributing. Everyone was on the pitch. Everyone showed he was willing to give everything for the team and for the shirt. The guys who were with us for the World Cup set the standards high, made everyone feel welcome and everyone had a good camp.

Industry observers note that he’s the best England player evert to wear the shirt and it’s an honour to play with him. And he’s only getting better.

In a recent development, A perfect night for me personally and also for the team. It’s been a tough camp, a long camp with some difficult games so it’s nice to finish it off all together. An extremely proud evening for me.

In a recent development, you saw some fantastic football out there tonight. The way we’re moving, the one-touch stuff, a fantastic ball from Elliot to Morgan and then a first time cross which was as good as it gets. As a striker you’re just waiting for those opportunities.

It started in the first game [reaching a higher level] although the result didn’t go for us. First game after a tournament, obviously this was a four-game camp, we had to find it [a higher level] and find it promptly. That’s the most pleasing thing.

This is the England team. There’s always going to be competition for places. It’s about taking the opportunity whether it’s 90 minutes, five minutes, whatever it was, make the most of it. You’re seeing that, everyone wants to be part of this. That’s only going to make us better for sure.

[Now for cap 126 next month?] That would be nice for sure.

In a recent development, shilton’s took him 20 years as Gordon Banks was simply too good in the couple of years following his debut and then a couple of managers, Don Revie and Ron Greenwood, preferred Ray Clemence until the latter finally plumped for Shilton as No 1 in 1979. Kane’s, by contrast, have taken him 11. In that time he has been rested for a handful of friendlies but has not been unused in a competitive match when fit since Gareth Southgate left him out of the 5-0 victory over Sam Marino in 2021’s World Cup qualifier when Dominic Calvert-Lewin scored two and Ollie Watkins one goal on his debut.

It has been revealed that england played the Czech Republic a week ago, winning 2-0 in Prague by virtue of Anthony Gordon’s cute header and Kane’s clever shot through a defender’s legs but they huffed and puffed for ages against a team harshly reduced to 10 men until they blew the house down. They went on to marmalise Croatia 7-0 in their next game in front of a crowd that sounded like a cross between the choirs on Another Brick in the Wall, Part 2 and There’s No One Quite Like Grandma.

According to recent reports, in the past England have had problems backing up their best performances – the 4-1 evisceration of the Dutch at Euro 96 was followed by the cagey display in the quarter-final against Spain before prevailing on penalties, the 5-1 victory in Munich in 2001 led to a drab 2-0 win against Albania at St James’ Park the following Tuesday, in 2016 they went to Berlin and beat world champions Germany but were thumped by Netherlands, who had not even qualified for Euro 2016, a couple of days later. Even their thrilling, second-half showing against Croatia in their World Cup opener in June preceded the dreary 0-0 draw with Ghana.

Given the attacking fluency in Rijeka, Thomas Tuchel must be tempted not to to ring the changes and replace seven or eight players. Ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers PGE2 production for tumour immune escape

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 77 min read (15391 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~77 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7.
  • Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15.
  • According to recent reports, potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ferroptosis, a form of cell death induced by overwhelming membrane lipid peroxidation, is a vulnerability of many cancers, including cancers resistant to current molecular and immune-based therapies1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Triggering of ferroptosis therefore provides an opportunity to achieve elimination of difficult-to-treat cancers1,2,3,4,8,9. Studies in mouse cancer models have demonstrated that anticancer immunity, mediated by dendritic cells (DCs) and CD8+ T cells, is essential for effective tumour eradication by ferroptosis-inducing strategies10,11,12,13. However, ferroptotic cells limit this response8,9,10,14, resulting in immune escape and tumour growth through mechanisms that remain unclear. Here we demonstrate that ferroptotic cancer cells activate a molecular program resulting in aberrant production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), which limits the stimulation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses by type 1 conventional DCs (cDC1s), thereby promoting immune escape. In ferroptotic cancer cells, lipid peroxidation-mediated membrane permeabilization enables Ca2+ influx, which activates p38 MAPK signalling and thereby drives PGE2 production. This signalling axis is uncoupled from cancer cell death and can be targeted to selectively interfere with immune-inhibitory PGE2 production while preserving ferroptotic cancer cell elimination. In the context of cancer cell ferroptosis, ablation of PGE2 production or disrupting PGE2 signalling restores cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell responses and leads to effective tumour elimination. Our findings identify a key mechanism that limits antitumour immunity and prevents tumour elimination upon ferroptosis induction in cancer cells, which could be exploited for cancer therapy.

Uncontrolled lipid peroxidation is integral to ferroptosis5,15. Cancer cells are commonly protected from unrestrained lipid peroxidation and spontaneous ferroptotic cell death by molecular defence systems such as the system xc––glutathione (GSH)–glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) pathway5,16, in which GPX4 is the key enzyme mediating lipid peroxide detoxification. Strategies to promote ferroptosis by blockade of ferroptosis defence systems, such as GPX4 inhibitors, have been considered promising approaches to achieve tumour elimination in patients with difficult-to-treat cancers8,9. Studies using preclinical mouse models have uncovered that effective tumour elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies requires anticancer immunity by DCs10 and tumour-infiltrating CD8+ T cells11,12,13. Yet recent findings have suggested that DC-driven anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity is suppressed in ferroptotic tumours8,9,10,17. Emerging evidence has implicated that the unrestrained generation of membrane lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells can promote the production and release of molecules that may impact immune cell functions18. However, what causes the suppression of DC-mediated anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity in the context of tumour ferroptosis remains largely unclear.

According to recent reports, potentially relevant immunoregulatory factors produced by ferroptotic cancer cells are oxylipins, bioactive lipids generated through peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane lipids, a hallmark of ferroptosis15. To assess ferroptosis-induced oxylipin production and identify key factors, we profiled the oxylipin secretome of mouse BRAF(V600E) and NRAS(G12D) melanoma, 4T1 breast cancer and MC38 colorectal cancer cells following RSL3-induced ferroptosis. Across all these cancer cell lines, RSL3-treated (ferroptotic) cells displayed increased production of oxylipins compared with untreated (non-ferroptotic) controls (Fig. 1a). Of note, in all groups, the eicosanoid PGE2 was by far the most abundant oxylipin upregulated by ferroptosis induction (Fig. 1a). Similar to ferroptosis induction by RSL3 (which inhibits selenoproteins beyond GPX4), we observed strong PGE2 production after genetic ablation of the ferroptosis-protective enzyme GPX4, ferroptosis induction using the GPX4 inhibitor ML210 or erastin-mediated inactivation of system xc–-mediated cystine import (Extended Data Fig. 1a–f). Thus, ferroptosis may trigger the production of PGE2 in cancer cells, which is a notable finding given the important role of PGE2 for suppression of anticancer immunity19,20,21.

In a recent development, by contrast, stimulation of ultraviolet B (UVB)-induced apoptosis, doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death or necrocide 1 (NC1)-induced necrotic cell death failed to promote PGE2 production (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1g). However, PGE2 production was induced in cells undergoing necroptosis (Extended Data Fig. 1h). These findings imply that PGE2 production is selectively induced by as yet unknown molecular events in ferroptotic cells and that these events, at least to some extent, may be shared with necroptotic cells.

Using liproxstatin-1 (Lip-1), we further validated that ferroptotic cancer cells depend on lipid peroxides to produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This was not the case for key effectors of other cell death pathways, such as caspases or receptor-interacting serine–threonine-protein kinase 1 (RIPK1; Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). We extended our analyses to a broader panel of mouse and human cancer cells, including established cell lines, cells from spontaneous mouse cancer models and cells from patients with pancreatic cancer. In all these cells, RSL3-induced ferroptosis triggered markedly increased PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). Together, these data suggest that ferroptosis promotes aberrant production of PGE2 in mouse and human cancer cells, prompting us to investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms and consequences for anticancer immunity.

Effective anticancer immunity often depends on cDC1s22,23, which fulfil essential roles in the priming of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses24,25 and effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ tumour-infiltrating T lymphocytes (TILs)26,27. These cDC1 functions are impacted by immunoregulatory factors derived from dying cancer cells22,23,28; however, how mediators released by ferroptotic cancer cells impact cDC1s and their functions is not known.

Industry observers note that to address this problem, we generated cDC1s from bone marrow cells, exposed them to conditioned medium from RSL3-induced, ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells and assessed their functional properties after activation with polyinosinic–polycytidylic acid (poly(I:C); Fig. 1c). The conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells strongly compromised the capacity of cDC1s to produce CXCL9 (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3a), a chemokine required for cDC1-mediated orchestration of CD8+ TIL responses26,29. Similar results were observed for cDC1 production of the T cell stimulatory cytokine interleukin-12 (IL-12)30 (Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). By contrast, no impairment was observed for cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from cancer cells undergoing apoptosis or doxorubicin-induced immunogenic cell death (Fig. 1d,e and Extended Data Fig. 3b,c). Impaired CXCL9 production was similarly observed for splenic cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 3d). These results suggest that factors released by ferroptotic cancer cells disable cDC1s from producing molecules required to promote anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity.

cDC1 functions are controlled by transcriptional programming31,32. We therefore subjected cDC1s activated by poly(I:C) following exposure to ferroptotic or apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cell conditioned medium to transcriptional profiling by RNA sequencing. We found that ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, cancer cell-derived factors induced prominent transcriptional changes in cDC1s (Fig. 1f), including impaired expression of genes encoding stimulatory cytokines (including Ifnb and Ifnl2), T cell-recruiting chemokines (Cxcl9 and Ccl4) and integrins crucial for T cell activation (Itgal; Fig. 1f). We also confirmed the inhibitory effect on cDC1 cytokine and chemokine production at the protein level (Extended Data Fig. 3e). Of note, we did not detect a defect in upregulation of MHC or costimulatory molecules (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Table 1), implying that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors do not prevent cDC1 activation. Of note, many of the genes impaired in cDC1s following exposure to ferroptotic cancer cell-derived factors were shared with a core gene set of PGE2-mediated cDC1 dysfunction (Extended Data Fig. 3f,g and Supplementary Table 1), although genes beyond this set were also impaired. Consistently, gene set enrichment analyses revealed a prominent impairment of PGE2-regulated functional cDC1 genes (Extended Data Fig. 3h), whereas genes associated with migration or antigen processing (that is, molecular programs not regulated by PGE2 signalling in cDC1s19), remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 3h). Together, these data suggest that ferroptotic cancer cells promote cDC1 dysfunction and that this is mediated by PGE2.

According to recent reports, similar to cancer cells, ferroptosis induction caused aberrant PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4a), an established mouse embryonic fibroblast model often used to study the molecular underpinnings of ferroptosis33. This was linked to markedly increased transcript and protein expression of the key PGE2-producing enzyme COX2 (encoded by Ptgs2; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 4b–d). Lip-1 treatment rescued this effect (Fig. 2a), whereas stimulation of lipid peroxidation by cumene hydroperoxide promoted both Ptgs2 expression and increased PGE2 production in Pfa1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Together, these results point towards a requirement of membrane lipid peroxide generation for PGE2 production through transcriptional regulation of COX2. Using COX inhibitors, we also confirmed that COX activity was required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2b), but dispensable for execution of ferroptotic cell death (Fig. 2c).

A key event caused by lipid peroxides in ferroptotic cells is the influx of extracellular Ca2+ (ref. 5), which constitutes an early event in pro-ferroptotic cells before the onset of cell death. Consistently, microscopy imaging revealed high intracellular Ca2+ levels in Pfa1 cells early after RSL3-mediated ferroptosis induction (Fig. 2d,e), which was similarly observed for multiple mouse cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4g,h). Time-resolved live cell imaging of ferroptotic Pfa1 cells confirmed that Ca2+ influx followed peroxide accumulation, but occurred before the cell death-associated loss of plasma membrane integrity (Fig. 2f). Of note, preventing Ca2+ influx through polyethylene glycol (PEG)-mediated blockade of membrane permeabilization-enabled osmotic molecule exchange5,34,35 (Fig. 2g and Extended Data Fig. 4i,j) abrogated the upregulation of Ptgs2 mRNA (Fig. 2h) and COX2 protein expression (Fig. 2i) in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells, resulting in a loss of PGE2 production (Fig. 2j). We also validated that lipid peroxide generation was only minimally affected by PEG treatment (Extended Data Fig. 4k,l) and that ferroptotic cells become permeable to other small extracellular molecules5, including sodium ions (Na+; Extended Data Fig. 4m–p).

It has been revealed that gain-of-function experiments using ionomycin, which selectively transport extracellular Ca2+ into cells, revealed that Ca2+ influx alone was sufficient to promote COX2 upregulation and PGE2 production across Pfa1, BRAF(V600E) melanoma and MC38 colorectal cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 4q,r). Thus, although small molecules beyond Ca2+ enter ferroptotic cells, they probably do not contribute substantially to the activation of COX-mediated PGE2 production. Consistently, blockade of Ca2+ influx using the Ca2+ chelator EGTA confirmed the relevance of Ca2+ signalling for PGE2 production in ferroptotic cells (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 4s,t).

Ca2+ influx can regulate gene expression via p38 MAPK signalling, which requires p38 MAPK activatory phosphorylation (p-p38). Consistently, ferroptotic Pfa1 cells displayed a prominent increase in p-p38 levels (Fig. 2l,m), which was abolished by PEG treatment (Fig. 2l,m). Moreover, treatment with the selective p38 MAPK inhibitor SB203580 abrogated the upregulation of COX2 expression and PGE2 production in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2n,o), demonstrating the relevance of p38 MAPK signalling for PGE2 production. Of note, the later execution of cell death remained unaffected by p38 MAPK inhibition (Fig. 2p) or blockade of Ca2+ influx (Extended Data Fig. 5a). These results suggest that Ca2+-induced p38 MAPK signalling is not required for ferroptotic cell death. We also confirmed that SB203580 did not induce cell death in non-ferroptotic cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a), and that the death of SB203580-treated ferroptotic Pfa1 cells was rescued by Lip-1 (Fig. 2q).

Sources indicate that oxylipin profiling revealed a selective requirement of p38 MAPK signalling for production of PGE2 and other COX-derived eicosanoids in ferroptotic Pfa1 cells (Fig. 2r), whereas other oxylipins remained largely unaffected. Similar to Pfa1 cells, PEG-mediated inhibition of Ca2+ influx or inhibition of p38 MAPK abolished PGE2 production in ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5b–e), demonstrating the relevance of Ca2+-mediated p38 MAPK pathway activation for PGE2 production also in ferroptotic cancer cells. We also confirmed that, in cancer cells, this mechanistic axis is already active in the early phase after ferroptosis induction (Extended Data Fig. 5f–r) and that p38 MAPK signalling is dispensable for the propagation of ferroptotic cell death (Extended Data Fig. 5s–v). Experiments with cells deficient in p38α (the p38 MAPK isoform commonly expressed in cancer cells) further validated that p38 MAPK signalling is required for PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells (Extended Data Fig. 5w,x), but not their cell death execution (Extended Data Fig. 5y). We conclude that Ca2+-mediated activation of p38 MAPK signalling triggers PGE2 production by ferroptotic cells and that this mechanism is not required for ferroptosis-dependent cancer cell death (Fig. 2s). This molecular uncoupling enables to selectively interfere with p38 MAPK pathway activity to impair PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells while preserving ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination.

According to recent reports, to test whether ferroptotic cancer cells depend on PGE2 to promote cDC1 dysfunction, we induced ferroptosis in COX-deficient Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells, which cannot produce PGE2 (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c). We then exposed cDC1s to conditioned medium from ferroptotic Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− or control BRAF(V600E) cells, activated them by poly(I:C) and compared their gene expression profile by RNA sequencing (Fig. 3a). We also included cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from apoptotic BRAF(V600E) cells, to test possible effects of dying cancer cell-derived factors unrelated to ferroptosis. We observed that PGE2 deficiency in ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells prevented cDC1 reprogramming (Fig. 3b) and, consequently, rescued the expression of functional cDC1 genes (for example, Irf8, Ifnl2 and Cxcl9; Fig. 3c). This regain of gene expression was similarly observed in a more detailed analysis of the core functional cDC1 genes selectively suppressed by factors from ferroptotic, but not apoptotic, BRAF(V600E) cells (Fig. 3d).

The inhibitory effect of PGE2 on immune cells36, including cDC1s19, is mediated by signalling through the PGE2 receptors EP2 (encoded by Ptger2) and EP4 (encoded by Ptger4). We therefore extended our RNA sequencing analyses to EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s from ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice19,26. Whereas conditioned medium from PGE2-producing ferroptotic control BRAF(V600E) cells compromised the upregulation of activation induced genes in (EP2/EP4-proficient) wildtype (WT) cDC1s, this defect was fully rescued in EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Table 2). This result demonstrates the relevance of PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling for ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated impairment of cDC1 functions. In separate experiments, we further validated that CXCL9 and IL-12 production is rescued in both EP2/EP4-deficient cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells and cDC1s treated with conditioned medium from (PGE2-deficient) ferroptotic Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− (BRAF(V600E)) cells (Fig. 3f,g and Extended Data Fig. 6d,e). Using CXCL9 as a functional marker, we also confirmed that PGE2 was similarly required for ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated inhibition of cDC1s activated by stimuli reported to promote cDC1 activation in tumours (Extended Data Fig. 6f,g). In a T cell stimulation assay, we further probed the ability of cDC1s to stimulate CD8+ T cell expansion. This function was similarly rescued in cDC1s exposed to conditioned medium from PGE2-deficient ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) cells (Fig. 3h,i). Using celecoxib (CXB)-mediated blockade of PGE2 production, we also confirmed that other ferroptotic cancer cells depend on PGE2 to inhibit cDC1 function, as determined by CXCL9 staining (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i). Together, these findings suggest that PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling mediates the impairment of cDC1 functions caused by ferroptotic cancer cells. Moreover, EP2/EP4 deficiency rescues cDC1s from ferroptotic cancer cell-mediated inhibition.

Our results raised the question whether cDC1s can mount effective CD8+ T cell responses against ferroptotic cancer cells when protected from inhibitory PGE2 signalling. To address this glitch, we adoptively transferred CD8+ OT-I T cells, which express a transgenic T cell receptor (TCR) specific for the model antigen ovalbumin (OVA), into WT mice subsequently transplanted with ferroptotic, OVA-expressing control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) cells (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To determine the relevance of EP2/EP4-mediated PGE2 signalling in cDC1, we further included Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, which lack EP2 and EP4 in CLEC9A-expressing cDC1. Analyses of OT-I T cell expansion in lymphoid tissues revealed that ferroptotic cancer cell-derived PGE2 impairs the productive generation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses through PGE2-mediated inhibition of cDC1 functions (Extended Data Fig. 7b–e). Moreover, OT-I T cell expansion was lost in cDC1-deficient Batf3−/− mice challenged with ferroptotic BRAF(V600E)–OVA cells (Extended Data Fig. 7f), confirming the functional relevance of cDC1s for generation of anticancer CD8+ T cell responses.

To determine whether ferroptotic tumours depend on PGE2 production to restrict cDC1-mediated anticancer CD8+ TIL responses and escape immune control, we analysed the growth of (ferroptotic) Gpx4−/− or (non-ferroptotic) WT MC38 cells transplanted into WT and Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4a). By microscopy-based analysis of the ferroptosis marker 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE) and COX2 protein, we confirmed cancer cell ferroptosis leading to enhanced COX pathway activity in Gpx4−/−, but not WT, MC38 tumours (Extended Data Fig. 8). In WT mice, tumours formed by Gpx4−/− MC38 cells exhibited progressive tumour growth, which was only minimally slower than WT MC38 cells (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). These data are consistent with inefficient control of ferroptotic cancers in immunocompetent mice. By contrast, Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice exhibited improved tumour immune control and fully rejected Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). By contrast, WT MC38 tumours displayed reduced growth but failed to be eliminated in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 9a). Of note, this pattern was similarly observed for Cd4crePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice in which T cells lack EP2/EP4 expression (Extended Data Fig. 9b), implying that ferroptotic tumours, in parallel to inhibiting cDC1, depend on PGE2-mediated inhibition of T cells to escape anticancer immunity.

In a recent development, we also genetically ablated p38α in Gpx4−/− MC38 cells, which disabled ferroptosis-induced PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 9c) and resulted in enhanced tumour growth control in WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 9d), consistent with the idea that p38 MAPK-induced PGE2 production by ferroptotic tumours promotes immune escape.

Of note, the efficient elimination of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice was linked to markedly increased intratumoural numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s (Fig. 4c), indicating their enhanced anticancer activity. By contrast, the numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s remained low in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, and in WT MC38 tumours in both WT and Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4c). Confocal immunofluorescence microscopy further revealed a prominent increase of interactive clusters between cDC1s and CD8+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f), pointing towards more productive cDC1-mediated instruction of anticancer CD8+ TIL responses19,26. Consistently, CD8+ TILs displayed substantially enhanced expansion in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice compared with all other groups (Fig. 4d,e).

cDC1s fulfil an essential role in anticancer immunity by driving the expansion and effector differentiation of TCF1+CD8+ TILs (often referred to as ‘stem-like’ T cells) into TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs with cytotoxic effector functions26. In many tumours, this process is critical for protective anticancer immunity37,38,39,40. The CD8+ TILs selectively accumulating in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice predominantly encompassed TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a) with high PD-1 and CXCR6 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10a), indicating more productive effector differentiation20,40. Consistently, TIM3+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice demonstrated markedly increased frequencies of cells expressing the cytotoxic effector molecule granzyme B (GZMB) compared with all other groups (Fig. 4g,h). We also confirmed that the numbers of stem-like TCF1+ TILs were comparable across all groups (Extended Data Fig. 10b), consistent with their unaffected tumour infiltration.

Of note, the few TIM3+CD8+ TILs detectable in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, similar to Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, displayed high expression of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 10c). This result indicates that CD8+ TILs, at least to some degree, mount proliferative responses also in ferroptotic tumours in the presence of intact PGE2 signalling on cDC1s. However, profiling of CD8+ TILs at later stages demonstrated that, in Gpx4−/− tumours in WT mice, these responses are not sustained over time, both in terms of Ki-67 expression, GZMB expression and CD8+ TIL expansion (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). By contrast, CD8+ TIL responses in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours further increased over time (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). Thus, only Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, but not WT mice, can mount protective CD8+ T cell immunity against ferroptotic tumours. By antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion, we further confirmed the relevance of CD8+ T cells for elimination of ferroptotic Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 10g–i).

It has been revealed that finally, to specifically examine whether pharmacological inhibition of COX-driven PGE2 production can achieve better immune control of ferroptotic tumours, we analysed the growth of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours transplanted into WT mice with or without CXB treatment. In line with PGE2-mediated impairment of anticancer immunity against ferroptotic tumours, Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in CXB-treated mice displayed markedly increased control of tumour growth (Fig. 4j). Of note, this effect was associated with prominently enhanced expansion of CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4k), with a high frequency of GZMB-expressing cells (Extended Data Fig. 10j). Similarly, tumours formed by Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells exhibited tumour regression in CXB-treated, but not in untreated, WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Consistent with these data, BRAF(V600E) melanoma tumour-bearing WT mice treated with a combination of CXB and the ferroptosis inducer imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) displayed enhanced tumour growth control compared with untreated mice or mice treated with CXB or IKE alone (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 10l). Together, these data suggest that PGE2 produced by ferroptotic cancer cells limits anticancer immunity by controlling cDC1-driven effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ TILs, which enables ferroptotic tumours to escape immune control. Interfering with the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis can elicit cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of CD8+ TILs in ferroptotic tumours and result in protective anticancer immunity.

Our results demonstrate that ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers aberrant synthesis of the bioactive lipid PGE2, enabling ferroptotic cancer cells to exert deleterious effects on cDC1-dependent, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity within tumour tissue. This inhibitory mechanism is critical for immune escape of ferroptotic tumours.

Beyond highlighting that tumour ferroptosis causes suppression of anticancer immunity, as has been recently suggested8,9,10,14,17, our results reveal that this barrier to ferroptosis-inducing strategies mechanistically depends on PGE2 and its signalling through the PGE2 receptors EP2 and EP4, preventing cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of anticancer CD8+ TILs. As a result, interference with PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling enhances the anticancer activity of cDC1s in ferroptotic tumours and induces protective, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity. These findings therefore identify a molecular mechanism fundamentally linked to the metabolic underpinnings of ferroptosis that may be decisive for ferroptosis-mediated impairment of cancer immunity. Of note, it seems likely that PGE2 from ferroptotic tumour cells not only targets cDC1s but in parallel also interferes directly with anticancer TILs, as indicated by our data. PGE2 may further limit the anticancer activity of other innate immune cells such as type 2 conventional DCs (cDC2s), monocyte–macrophages or natural killer cells41.

We have revealed that PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells involves p38 MAPK signalling activated through lipid peroxidation-induced, membrane permeabilization-dependent Ca2+ influx, which activates a molecular program that causes transcriptional upregulation of the COX–PGE2 pathway. Beyond providing a mechanistic explanation for high COX2 levels in ferroptotic cells, as has been recently observed18,42, our results uncover that this trait acquired by ferroptotic cells is uncoupled from the execution of cell death. As a consequence, interference with p38 MAPK signalling can disable the production of PGE2 while maintaining effective cancer cell elimination by ferroptosis inducers.

Multiple studies have highlighted the vulnerability of therapy-resistant and difficult-to-treat cancers to ferroptosis induction and the dependency of ferroptotic cancer elimination on anticancer immunity. Therefore, our discoveries that ferroptotic tumour cells antagonize anticancer immunity through the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis and the uncoupling of this mechanism from ferroptosis-mediated tumour cell elimination have vital mechanistic and clinical implications. Our results indicate that targeting PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling to overcome ferroptosis-induced immunosuppression may provide an attractive means to unleash anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity and achieve cancer elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. On this note, abolishing PGE2 production by inhibition of p38 MAPK signalling bears the potential to interfere with the immunosuppressive capacity of ferroptotic cancer cells without curbing ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination. Our findings therefore identify p38 MAPK signalling-induced COX–PGE2 pathway activity in ferroptotic cancer cells as a potential molecular target to prevent immune evasion and improve cancer therapy by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. Of note, disabling the p38 MAPK–COX–PGE2 signalling may further benefit necroptosis-inducing strategies, as indicated by our findings with necroptotic cells.

Ptger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice were generated by crossing Ptger2−/− mice (004376, JAX) to Ptger4fl/fl mice (028102, JAX) and further crossed to Clec9acre mice (025523, JAX) to generate Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, crossed to Cd4cre mice (022071, JAX) to generate Cd4crePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice or crossed to Itgaxcre mice (008068, JAX) to generate ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice. Recent findings suggest that control and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells were generated using the CRISPR–Cas9 system as previously described21. BRAF(V600E)–OVA and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA variants were generated by lentiviral transduction, as previously described20. 4-OH-TAM-inducible Gpx4−/− mouse immortalized fibroblasts (Pfa1) have been previously described43. Gpx4−/− MC38 and Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector expressing single guide RNAs, as previously described44. In brief, Gpx4-targeting single guide RNA (5′-caccGCGTGTGCATCGTCACCAACG) was cloned in the BsmBI-digested lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector (98290, Addgene) and used to transiently transfect cancer cell lines using the X-tremeGENE HP agent (Roche). One day after transfection, cells were selected using puromycin (5 µg ml−1) and further cultivated with Lip-1 (1 µM) to prevent ferroptosis. After selection, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. Mapk14−/− cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the p38α MAPK14 CRISPR–Cas9 knockout plasmid (sc-424051; Santa Cruz) according to manufacturer’s protocol. After sorting for GFP+ cells, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. BRAF(V600E), Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E), BRAF(V600E)–OVA, Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA, 4T1, NRAS(G12D), LLC, CT26, SLCL, Pfa1, NIH3T3, A549, Su86.86 and HT-29 cells were cultured in complete RPMI medium (RPMI 1640 medium, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS (PAN-Biotech), 50 U ml–1 penicillin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 µg ml–1 streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). MC38, D4M.3 A, Panc02, mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and human patient-derived PDAC cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS, 50 U ml–1 penicillin and 50 mg ml–1 streptomycin. Gpx4−/− cells were cultured in their respective medium supplemented with 1 μM Lip-1 to prevent ferroptosis. For in vitro assays, Gpx4−/− cell lines were cultivated in 1 µM Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) for one passage before seeding them with or without Fer-1 to assess ferroptosis and PGE2 production. Unless stated otherwise, all analyses of cell viability and PGE2 production were performed after 24 h.

In a recent development, to generate cancer cell conditioned medium, 4 × 105 cancer cells were cultured in 2 ml complete RPMI medium or DMEM for 24 h before addition of the ferroptosis inducers RSL3 or ML210 (250 nM for NRAS(G12D), 500 nM for 4T1 and D4M.3A, and 1,000 nM for BRAF(V600E) and MC38 cells), doxorubicin (10 µM) or treatment with 150 mJ cm−2 UVB. 8 h later, cancer cells were washed three times with PBS and cultivated for another 16 h in complete RPMI or DMEM. The cell supernatant was collected, centrifuged at 600g for 5 min to remove dead cell debris and stored at −20 °C until further use. All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination in-house by PCR. No further cell line authentications were conducted in the laboratory.

In a recent development, cancer cell lines were detached by trypsinization (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and washed three times in sterile PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were injected subcutaneously in 100 μl endotoxin-free PBS on the flank of recipient mice, using 2 × 105 cells for tumour growth studies and 2 × 106 cells for all other experiments. Tumour growth was measured using a digital calliper. Tumour diameters stated in the figures refer to the average values of the longest diameter and its perpendicular for each tumour. Tumour growth was restricted to a maximum diameter of 15 mm, which served as the humane end point and was not exceeded in any of the experiments. For animals reaching the humane end point before the end of the observation period, the last measured tumour diameter was carried forwards to subsequent time points (last observation carried forwards). For experiments involving ferroptotic control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA melanoma cells, cancer cells were pre-treated with 1 μM RSL3 for 8 h before subcutaneous injection of 1 × 106 cells in 100 μl of endotoxin-free PBS into the flank of recipient mice.

To deplete CD8+ T cells, mice received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl anti-mouse CD8β antibody (200 µg per mouse; 53-5.8, BioXCell) every 5 days, beginning on day 1 following tumour cell inoculation.

Industry observers note that treatment of mice bearing subcutaneous MC38 or control BRAF(V600E) tumours was initiated once tumours were palpable, on days 3–5 post-tumour cell transplantation. Solutions were prepared fresh every day. For induction of ferroptosis, mice received daily intraperitoneal injection of 40 mg kg−1 IKE dissolved in 55% PEG 300 (Sigma) and 45% PBS. Lyophilized CXB (MedChem) was weighed using a fine balance and made up in a 60:40 ratio of DMSO (1 part, Sigma)/PEG400 (5 parts, Sigma):dH2O. The final concentration was 6 mg ml−1, corresponding to a dose of 30 mg kg−1 delivered in a total volume of 100 µl per mouse. CXB was administered daily by oral gavage.

Sources indicate that tumours, lymph nodes or spleens of tumour cell-inoculated mice were collected at the indicated time points after cancer cell transplantation. Tumour or organ weight was measured using a microscale. For flow cytometry analysis, tumour samples were mechanically dissociated and digested with DNase I (100 µg ml–1, Merck) and collagenase IV (200 U ml–1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 40 min at 37 °C followed by filtration through a 70-µm and a 30-µm cell strainer (Miltenyi) and washing with FACS buffer (PBS with 1% FCS and 2 mM EDTA) to generate single-cell suspensions before proceeding with antibody-mediated staining. Spleens were passed through a 70-µm cell strainer, followed by red blood cell lysis with ACK-lysis buffer for 3 min and additional filtration using a 30-µm cell strainer. Lymph nodes were dissociated using a 30-µm cell strainer.
